🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.69% (intraday, 7-year +24bp). The biggest story this morning is oil. Brent is at 104.96 (+4.76 on the session) and WTI is at 92.54 (+4.26) after reports that the White House is weighing renewed large-scale strikes on Iran before the Nov 3 midterms. Talks over reopening the Strait of Hormuz are at an impasse (CBS News). Pre-market, ES futures are down 35.25 at 7817.5, NQ is down 230.75 and Dow futures are down 356.0. That extends yesterday's soft cash session: SPX -17.16 to 7801.77, Dow -341.41 and Russell 2000 -37.093 (small caps hit hardest). Europe is also lower: Euro Stoxx 50 -48.05 and STOXX 600 -3.53. The Nikkei fell 993.6. Yields are adding pressure, with the US 2Y +4.4bp to 4.8122%, the 10Y +3.2bp to 5.3157% and the 30Y at 5.6831%. The 10Y is 8.78% above its 50-day average with a computed z-score of 2.21, at a 100th-percentile rank. VIX rose 0.63 to 15.71, which is still low. The second story is under the surface in credit. The Bloomberg Caa–B gap (how much more the weakest junk issuers pay than single-B issuers) is 707bp. That is the 100th percentile of its 5-year range and the widest since 2020-04-27, up 83bp in a month and 195bp over 3 months, versus a 5-year average of about 409bp. The FRED cross-check shows the same thing: CCC–B is at 912bp, in the 100th percentile. Is the CCC stress spreading upward? Partly. Over the past month single-B widened 40bp to 291bp and Ba widened 32bp to 184bp, and HY–IG widened 38bp. Both are still below their 5-year averages (B about 348bp, Ba about 219bp), and both tightened last week (B -10, Ba -2). The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily spread changes rose to 0.52 from 0.30 a month ago and 0.20 three months ago. Weak-tier moves are increasingly dragging single-B along, but the correlation is still below its 5-year median of 0.70. Investment grade is untouched at 80bp (0 change over 1m). This is descriptive, not a validated signal. Read it as rot that is starting to leak up the ladder but has not breached BB/IG levels. Sentiment is risk-off at the margin: oil up, yields up, small caps and cyclicals (Industrials -2.14%, Materials -1.53% on the day) leading lower, and defensives such as Health Care (+1.06%) bid.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.92 vol points (70th percentile of the 37 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 102.6 (74th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 114bp (steeper by 37bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 77% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (84bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.32 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 77%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Sticky but slowly cooling underlying inflation, with the oil shock as an upside risk. Every core-trend measure is labeled 'falling' in the computed panel, and the levels are mid-range relative to history. Breadth is uneven: in the Dallas Fed distribution, 13.2% of the PCE basket is rising >10% and 15.7% is rising 5-10%, while 25.8% is falling. Core PCE at 3.00759 is still well above target. With Brent above $100 and 1y breakevens (2.84) above 5y (2.4148), near-term inflation expectations are the vulnerable part, which supports the Fed's hiking bias.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

On the computed path chart, the current rally (anchored Oct-2022) is at 250.6 in month 48, slightly ahead of the dot-com run anchored at the Oct-1990 bottom, which was 235.7 at month 48 and did not peak until month 113. History therefore says a rally of this shape can run much further, but the valuation marker (23%) shows today's multiples are nowhere near the 2000 extreme for the Nasdaq. The external valuation gauges are more worrying. Shiller CAPE is around 41, the highest since the dot-com peak. The Buffett indicator is about 236-237% of GDP, and the top-10 weight is about 35% of the S&P 500 (all analyst estimates from cited reporting). The combination of extremely tight spreads, low VIX, loose financial conditions, a 5.3% 10Y and a Fed in a hiking cycle resembles 1999-2000 more in its catalysts than in its froth. The 2000 drawdown (Nasdaq -78% over 31 months) followed Fed tightening into tight credit. The HY low-tier stress emerging now is the kind of crack the catalyst dimension is built to flag. IPO froth is subdued (mostly small biotech and SPAC deals this week), so ipo_froth_pct is set low; lt_eps_growth_pct is a judgment estimate, not sourced.

⚔️Iran War

According to CBS News live coverage, The Atlantic reported that President Trump is considering resuming strikes on Iran before the Nov 3 midterms, and Brent jumped above $105 on the report. The Pentagon has reportedly told CENTCOM to finish preparations for major combat operations, but no decision or date is set. Diplomacy is stalled. After Trump rejected Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Iran said it was reviewing the US response, and its foreign minister said there is no military solution. Pakistan, Oman, Qatar and Egypt are still mediating. Iran reportedly stepped up strikes on tankers in Hormuz. A June deal that reopened the strait collapsed in July, and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports is reported in place. Houthi forces claimed a third missile strike this week on Saudi Arabia's main airport. Earlier in the week oil had eased on signs Gulf exports were recovering toward pre-war levels and on G7 agreement to release stockpiles, and today's move reverses that. Caveat: sources disagree on whether major combat has already resumed. One unofficial tracker says it has, while CBS describes a recent US shift toward economic pressure. Treat the war status as unconfirmed.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inference: a 25bp hike at the next FOMC is slightly more likely than a hold. The September dot plot shows one more hike this year (median 4.1%), core PCE is at 3.0 and oil is spiking. Warsh has said inflation is not falling fast enough. However, he has abandoned forward guidance, so he will not pre-signal, and he held in July despite pressure, which shows he is willing to wait. The next meeting date was not verified in this session.

~1 YEAR

Inference: policy rate around 4.0-4.25% with a bias to hold once the hiking cycle ends. Cuts would require a clear decline in core PCE toward the median/trimmed-mean measures (about 2.2-2.6). A credit event such as low-tier HY stress spreading to BB/IG, or an oil-driven growth shock, is the main path to an earlier pivot. This view is inferred, not stated by Warsh.

Warsh's Fed held at 3.50-3.75% at his first meeting in June and again in July, a decision CNBC said raised credibility questions as yields rose. On Sept 16 the Fed then hiked unanimously (12-0) to 3.75-4.00%, the first hike since 2023, with Warsh saying inflation is still too high. He has said he is 'not in the forward guidance business' and defended the hikes against Trump's criticism. His on-record pattern is to act on realized inflation rather than signal in advance and to tolerate political friction. Combined with Brent above $100, a 2Y at 4.8122% and 1y breakevens at 2.84, that argues for a hawkish lean. Flagged inference: his long-standing preference for a smaller Fed balance sheet is from his prior public record and was not re-verified with a URL in this session.
